title: Covalent bonding: molecules, polymers and giant structures

steps.title: Sharing electrons
steps.body: Two non-metal atoms both want a full outer shell, and neither will give electrons up. So they **share**: a shared pair of electrons is a **covalent bond**. Hydrogen chloride shares one pair. The shared electrons count towards both atoms.

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for hydrogen chloride: hydrogen and chlorine sharing one pair of electrons

steps.text: Hydrogen has 1 outer electron and needs 2; chlorine has 7 and needs 8
They share one pair: put the hydrogen's dot and one of the chlorine's crosses in the overlap
steps.note: one shared pair is one covalent bond

steps.text: Count for hydrogen: 2 electrons. Count for chlorine: the shared pair plus its three lone pairs, so 8
steps.note: a shared pair counts for both atoms

steps.text: Eight electrons are drawn in all, 1 from hydrogen and 7 from chlorine: sharing creates none
steps.note: check the total before you stop

check.prompt: Which pair of elements bonds covalently?
check.solution: Two non-metals share electrons. Metal with non-metal is ionic; two metals is metallic.
options: Hydrogen and oxygen
Sodium and chlorine
Magnesium and oxygen
Iron and copper

steps.title: Double and triple bonds
steps.body: Oxygen atoms need two more electrons each, so two oxygen atoms share **two pairs**: a double bond, O=O. Nitrogen atoms need three, so N₂ has a **triple bond**. Count the outer electrons: each atom should end up with eight (hydrogen with two).

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for oxygen: two oxygen atoms sharing two pairs of electrons, a double bond

visuals.problem: Draw the dot-and-cross diagram for nitrogen, N₂, and check the electron count.

steps.text: Each nitrogen has 5 outer electrons and needs 3 more
Share 3 pairs: 3 electrons from each atom go into the overlap
Each atom now has 3 shared pairs (6 electrons) plus its own lone pair (2 electrons), making 8
Total electrons drawn = 10, the same as 5 + 5: sharing creates nothing and loses nothing

check.prompt: How many pairs of electrons are shared in a molecule of nitrogen, N₂? Give your answer as a number.
check.solution: Each nitrogen needs three more electrons: a triple bond, **3** shared pairs.

steps.title: Drawing a dot-and-cross diagram
steps.body: Outer shells only. Use dots for one atom and crosses for the other so the examiner can see where each electron came from.

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for water: an oxygen atom sharing one pair with each of two hydrogen atoms, with two lone pairs on the oxygen

steps.text: Oxygen has 6 outer electrons; each hydrogen has 1
Oxygen shares one pair with each hydrogen: two single bonds
Oxygen ends with 8 (2 shared pairs plus 2 lone pairs); each hydrogen ends with 2

steps.title: Ammonia and methane
steps.body:
Nitrogen has five outer electrons and needs three more, so it bonds to three hydrogens. That uses three of its five electrons, leaving one **lone pair** on the nitrogen. Forgetting that lone pair is the most common slip in this diagram.

Carbon has four outer electrons and needs four more, so methane has four single bonds and no lone pairs on the carbon.

Molecules can be drawn in several ways, and each one hides something. A **dot-and-cross diagram** shows where every outer electron came from, but not the shape. A **ball-and-stick model** shows the shape and the bond angles, but the sticks make the bonds look like solid rods and the shared pairs of electrons are not shown at all. A **space-filling model** shows how much room the atoms really take up, but hides the bonds inside. A **displayed formula** is quick to draw but is flat, when methane is really tetrahedral.

visuals.alt: Dot-and-cross diagram for ammonia: a nitrogen atom sharing one pair with each of three hydrogen atoms, with one lone pair on the nitrogen
Dot-and-cross diagram for methane: a carbon atom sharing one pair with each of four hydrogen atoms

steps.text: Nitrogen has 5 outer electrons; each hydrogen has 1
Nitrogen shares one pair with each of three hydrogens: three single bonds
Nitrogen ends with 8 (3 shared pairs plus 1 lone pair); each hydrogen ends with 2

steps.title: Simple molecules: strong inside, weak between
steps.body: Substances like water, oxygen, methane and chlorine are **simple molecules**: a few atoms held together by **strong covalent bonds**. But the forces **between** molecules, the **intermolecular forces**, are **weak**. Melting or boiling separates the molecules; it does **not** break the covalent bonds. Weak forces need little energy to overcome, so simple molecular substances have **low melting and boiling points**, and are often gases or liquids.

visuals.alt: Simple molecules: pairs of atoms strongly bonded, scattered with weak forces between the molecules

visuals.problem: Explain why oxygen is a gas at room temperature. (3 marks)

steps.text: Oxygen is made of small O₂ molecules: a simple molecular substance
The intermolecular forces between the molecules are weak
Only a little energy is needed to overcome them, so the boiling point is far below room temperature. The covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken.

check.prompt: When water boils, what is overcome?
check.solution: The molecules stay intact; they just separate from each other.
options: The weak intermolecular forces between water molecules
The covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen
The ionic bonds
The metallic bonds

steps.title: Bigger molecules, higher boiling points
steps.body:
Intermolecular forces grow with the size of the molecule. Methane (CH₄) is a gas, octane (C₈H₁₈) is a liquid, and candle wax (around C₃₀) is a solid. **Polymers** are the extreme: chains of thousands of atoms, so the intermolecular forces add up to enough to make them solids at room temperature.

Simple molecules **do not conduct** electricity: they have no overall charge and no free electrons.

visuals.alt: A polymer: a very long chain of carbon atoms joined by covalent bonds, with bonds to side atoms shown

visuals.problem: Which has the higher boiling point, ethane C₂H₆ or hexane C₆H₁₄? Explain your answer.

steps.text: Both are simple molecules with weak intermolecular forces
Hexane molecules are larger, so the intermolecular forces between them are stronger
More energy is needed to separate hexane molecules, so hexane has the higher boiling point: 69 °C, against −89 °C for ethane

check.prompt: Which has the highest boiling point?
check.solution: The largest molecule has the largest intermolecular forces.
options: C₈H₁₈
CH₄
C₂H₆
C₄H₁₀

steps.title: Giant covalent structures
steps.body: In **diamond**, **graphite**, and **silicon dioxide** there are no molecules. Every atom is covalently bonded to its neighbours in a **giant lattice**. To melt one, the **covalent bonds themselves** must be broken, and there are millions of them, so melting points are **very high** and they are solids. Diamond and silicon dioxide do not conduct: all their outer electrons are held in bonds. Graphite is the one exception, because each carbon bonds to only three others and the spare electron is delocalised. You meet that in the topic on diamond, graphite and graphene.

visuals.alt: A giant covalent structure: a continuous network of atoms joined by covalent bonds

visuals.problem: Explain why silicon dioxide (sand) does not conduct electricity, even when molten.

steps.text: It is a giant covalent structure: every silicon and oxygen atom is held in the lattice by covalent bonds
All the outer electrons are used in those bonds, so none are delocalised
There are no ions either, so even when molten there are no charged particles free to move

check.prompt: Why does silicon dioxide have a much higher melting point than carbon dioxide?
check.skill: comparing giant covalent with simple molecular
check.solution: Giant covalent versus simple molecular: the forces overcome are different in kind.
options: Melting silicon dioxide breaks many strong covalent bonds; melting carbon dioxide only overcomes weak intermolecular forces
Silicon dioxide has much stronger intermolecular forces than carbon dioxide because its molecules are heavier
Carbon dioxide has no covalent bonds at all, so there is nothing to break when it turns into a gas
Silicon dioxide is ionic, so strong electrostatic forces between its ions must be overcome to melt it

steps.title: Your turn: which structure?
steps.body: Read the properties and name the structure. Low melting point and no conduction: **simple molecules**. Very high melting point and no conduction: **giant covalent**. High melting point, conducts only when molten or dissolved: **ionic**. **Conducts when solid: a metal** — or graphite, the one giant covalent structure that conducts, told apart by its very high melting point.

visuals.problem: A substance melts at 1710 °C and never conducts

steps.text: Very high melting point: a giant structure
Never conducts, even molten: not ionic, not a metal
Giant covalent, such as silicon dioxide

check.prompt: A substance melts at −23 °C and does not conduct electricity. Its structure is
check.solution: A low melting point means weak forces between particles: molecules.
options: simple molecular
giant covalent
giant ionic
metallic

steps.title: Going deeper: the sentence examiners are waiting for
steps.body:
The single most common slip in this topic is saying a simple molecular substance has a low boiling point "because the covalent bonds are weak". They are not. The answer is: **the intermolecular forces are weak, and the covalent bonds inside the molecules are not broken**. Write both halves.

Top questions also ask you to **compare** two substances with the same bonding but different structures, such as CO₂ and SiO₂, or methane and poly(ethene). Name the structure, name the forces overcome, then say how much energy that needs.

steps.text: Both: covalent bonds between atoms
CO₂: simple molecules; boiling overcomes weak intermolecular forces; little energy; gas
SiO₂: giant covalent; melting breaks many strong covalent bonds; lots of energy; solid

check.prompt: Ethane and poly(ethene) both contain only C–C and C–H bonds. Why is one a gas and the other a solid?
check.solution: Same bonds, same kind of intermolecular force, but thousands of times more of it along the chain.

markScheme.description: Longer molecules, larger total intermolecular forces

options: Poly(ethene) molecules are far longer, so the intermolecular forces between them are far larger in total
Poly(ethene) has far stronger covalent bonds, so far more energy is needed to pull its atoms apart
Methane has no intermolecular forces at all, so its molecules can never stick together as a solid
Poly(ethene) is a giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must break for it to melt

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Covalent bond: a shared pair of electrons between non-metal atoms. Double and triple bonds share two or three pairs.
- Simple molecules: strong covalent bonds inside, weak intermolecular forces between. Low melting and boiling points; no conduction.
- Bigger molecules, stronger intermolecular forces. Polymers are long enough to be solids.
- Giant covalent: every atom bonded in a lattice; very high melting points because covalent bonds must break.
- Say "the intermolecular forces are weak", not "the covalent bonds are weak". The bonds inside a molecule are strong and stay intact.

visuals.alt: A giant covalent lattice: every atom joined to its neighbours by covalent bonds
Simple molecules for contrast: strong bonds inside, weak forces between

questions.solution: Covalent bonding is sharing. Transfer is ionic; the sea of electrons is metallic.
options: a shared pair of electrons between two non-metal atoms
the transfer of electrons from a metal to a non-metal
the attraction between a positive ion and a sea of electrons
a weak force between molecules

questions.prompt: How many shared pairs of electrons are there in a molecule of oxygen, O₂? Give your answer as a number.
questions.solution: Each oxygen atom needs two more electrons, so they share two pairs: a double bond. **2** shared pairs.

questions.prompt: Which substance is made of simple molecules?
questions.solution: Water is a small molecule of three atoms. Sodium chloride is a giant ionic lattice, diamond a giant covalent structure, copper a metal.
options: Water, H₂O
Sodium chloride, NaCl
Diamond
Copper

questions.prompt: Why does chlorine, Cl₂, have a low boiling point?
questions.solution: Boiling separates molecules from each other. It does not break the covalent bonds inside them, which stay intact.
options: The intermolecular forces between the molecules are weak, so little energy is needed to separate them
The covalent bonds between the two chlorine atoms are weak, so little energy is needed to break them
The molecules have very few electrons, so there is almost nothing holding them together
Chlorine has a giant structure with many weak bonds that all break at a low temperature

questions.prompt: Which statement about the boiling points of small molecules is correct?
questions.solution: Intermolecular forces grow with the size of the molecule, so bigger molecules need more energy to separate.
options: Larger molecules have stronger intermolecular forces, so higher boiling points
Larger molecules have stronger covalent bonds, so higher boiling points
All small molecules boil at the same temperature
Smaller molecules have higher boiling points

questions.prompt: Explain why diamond has a very high melting point.
questions.solution: For giant covalent structures the bonds themselves break on melting, so "strong covalent bonds" is the right phrase here, unlike for simple molecules.

markScheme.description: Each carbon bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds
Many strong bonds to break, lots of energy

criteria.text: Diamond is a giant covalent structure
Every carbon atom is bonded to four others by strong covalent bonds
Many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it, which needs a very large amount of energy

questions.modelAnswer: Diamond is a giant covalent structure in which every carbon atom is joined to four others by strong covalent bonds. To melt it, many of these strong covalent bonds must be broken, which needs a very large amount of energy, so the melting point is very high.

questions.prompt: Why do most covalent substances not conduct electricity?
questions.solution: Conduction needs charged particles that can move. Molecules are neutral and their electrons are held in bonds.
options: They have no free electrons or ions to carry charge
Their covalent bonds are too strong for a current to pass
They are all gases, and gases cannot carry a current
They dissolve in water, which stops the current flowing

questions.prompt: Poly(ethene) is a polymer. Which statement is correct?
questions.solution: Polymers are very long molecules. The intermolecular forces add up along the chain, so they are solids, though still with covalent bonds inside each chain.

markScheme.description: Long molecules, relatively strong intermolecular forces

options: It is a solid at room temperature because its long molecules have relatively strong intermolecular forces
It is a gas at room temperature because it is made of molecules, and molecular substances are gases
It is a solid because its atoms are held in a giant ionic lattice by strong electrostatic forces
It is a solid because the atoms along each chain are held together by weak intermolecular forces

questions.prompt: Compare the structure and bonding of silicon dioxide with that of carbon dioxide, and explain why silicon dioxide is a solid with a high melting point while carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature.
questions.skill: comparing giant covalent with simple molecular
questions.solution: Level-marked. The mark is in saying which forces are overcome in each case: bonds for the giant structure, intermolecular forces for the molecules.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about the two structures and the forces overcome on melting or boiling, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of the two structures and the forces overcome on melting or boiling with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of the two structures and the forces overcome on melting or boiling using the correct terms

criteria.text: Both contain covalent bonds between atoms
Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure: every silicon atom bonded to four oxygen atoms in a lattice
Carbon dioxide is made of simple molecules, each of one carbon and two oxygen atoms with double bonds
To melt silicon dioxide many strong covalent bonds must be broken, needing a lot of energy
To turn carbon dioxide into a gas only the weak intermolecular forces between molecules are overcome; the covalent bonds inside the molecules do not break
So little energy is needed for carbon dioxide and a great deal for silicon dioxide

questions.modelAnswer: Both substances contain strong covalent bonds. Silicon dioxide is a giant covalent structure in which each silicon atom is bonded to four oxygen atoms, and each oxygen to two silicon atoms, in a continuous lattice. Carbon dioxide is made of simple molecules, each a carbon atom double-bonded to two oxygen atoms. Melting silicon dioxide means breaking many strong covalent bonds, which needs a great deal of energy, so the melting point is high. Turning carbon dioxide into a gas only means overcoming the weak intermolecular forces between the molecules; the covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact. That takes little energy, so carbon dioxide is a gas at room temperature.

questions.prompt: A student says "water boils at 100 °C because the covalent bonds between hydrogen and oxygen are weak". What is wrong with this?
questions.solution: The classic error. Covalent bonds inside a molecule are strong. Boiling is about the weak forces between molecules.
options: Boiling separates molecules by overcoming intermolecular forces; the O–H covalent bonds are strong and do not break
Water does not contain covalent bonds; the hydrogen and oxygen are held together by ionic bonds instead
Water boils because it is ionic, and boiling separates the hydrogen ions from the oxide ions
Nothing is wrong: the O–H bonds are weak, which is why water boils at such a low temperature

questions.prompt: Which dot-and-cross diagram is correct for nitrogen, N₂?
questions.solution: Each nitrogen has five outer electrons and needs three more. Three shared pairs (a triple bond) plus one lone pair each gives both atoms eight.

markScheme.description: Triple bond and one lone pair each

options: Three shared pairs between the atoms, with one non-bonding pair left on each nitrogen
One shared pair between the atoms, with three non-bonding pairs left on each nitrogen
Two shared pairs between the atoms, with two non-bonding pairs left on each nitrogen
Three shared pairs between the atoms, with no other electrons on either nitrogen

questions.prompt: Methane has the formula CH₄. How many covalent bonds does each carbon atom form, and how many electrons are in the outer shell of the carbon atom in the molecule? Give your answer as two numbers separated by a comma, bonds first.
questions.solution: Carbon has four outer electrons and shares each with a hydrogen: four bonds. Four shared pairs give the carbon eight outer electrons.
accepted: 4 bonds and 8 electrons in the outer shell

questions.prompt: Hydrogen chloride, HCl, is a gas that dissolves in water to make an acidic solution that conducts electricity. Pure liquid hydrogen chloride does not conduct. Explain these observations.
questions.solution: Links bonding to conduction and to acids, which is the kind of cross-topic reasoning that separates grade 9.

markScheme.description: Covalent molecule, no free charged particles when pure
Ionises in water to H⁺ and Cl⁻

criteria.text: HCl is a simple covalent molecule, so pure HCl has no ions or free electrons and cannot conduct
In water the molecules split (ionise) into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
The ions are free to move in the solution, so it conducts
The H⁺ ions make the solution acidic

questions.modelAnswer: Hydrogen chloride is a simple covalent molecule. As a pure liquid it contains no ions and no free electrons, so there is nothing to carry charge and it does not conduct. When it dissolves in water, the molecules split into hydrogen ions, H⁺, and chloride ions, Cl⁻. These ions are free to move through the solution, so it conducts, and the H⁺ ions are what make it acidic.

questions.prompt: Which of these best explains why polymers such as poly(ethene) are solids at room temperature but small alkanes such as ethane are gases, even though both contain only C–H and C–C covalent bonds?
questions.solution: Same bonds, same type of intermolecular force, but far more of it along a long chain. That is why polymers are solids.

markScheme.description: Much longer molecules, larger total intermolecular forces

options: The polymer molecules are very much longer, so the intermolecular forces between them are much larger in total
The polymer has much stronger covalent bonds along its chain, so much more energy is needed to melt it
The polymer is a giant covalent structure, so many strong covalent bonds must be broken to melt it
Methane has no intermolecular forces at all, so its molecules never stick together to form a solid

questions.prompt: A ball-and-stick model of methane shows sticks joining the balls. What is the main limitation of this model?
questions.solution: Models simplify. Sticks make bonds look like solid rods and hide the shared electrons; a dot-and-cross diagram shows the electrons but not the shape.

markScheme.description: Bonds shown as rods, shared electrons not shown

options: It suggests the bonds are solid rods and does not show the shared pairs of electrons
It shows the wrong number of hydrogen atoms because the balls are all the same size
It cannot show that methane is a gas, because the model is made of solid parts
It cannot show which atoms are carbon and which are hydrogen, because every ball is drawn the same

questions.prompt: A ball-and-stick model shows one carbon atom joined to two oxygen atoms by double bonds. Give the molecular formula of the substance.
questions.solution: One carbon and two oxygens: CO₂, carbon dioxide.

questions.prompt: Hydrogen sulfide has the formula H₂S. Sulfur is in Group 6. How many lone pairs of electrons are on the sulfur atom in the molecule?
questions.solution: Sulfur has six outer electrons. Two are used in bonds to hydrogen, leaving four, which is two lone pairs. The same pattern as water, because sulfur sits below oxygen in Group 6.

examTechnique.body: Covalent bonding questions test one distinction above all: bonds inside molecules against forces between them. Say "weak intermolecular forces" for simple molecules and "many strong covalent bonds must be broken" for giant covalent structures. Dot-and-cross diagrams show outer shells only, with shared pairs in the overlap.
examinerErrors: Saying the covalent bonds are weak in a simple molecular substance.
Saying bonds are broken when a molecular substance melts or boils.
Forgetting lone pairs on oxygen, nitrogen, or chlorine in a dot-and-cross diagram.
Calling a polymer a giant covalent structure. It is a very long molecule.
Explaining that a substance does not conduct "because it is covalent" without saying there are no free charged particles.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer names the structure before explaining any property, says which forces are overcome and how strong they are, keeps the covalent bonds intact when a molecular substance changes state, and can compare two substances with the same bonding but different structures.
